item.title: AI Compute 12: The Build-Out Is a Bet on Reinforcement Learning
item.description: The AI build-out, hundreds of billions of dollars of chips, buildings, and power, rests on demand continuing to grow, and most of that demand is the frontier labs consuming their own compute to train the next model. Whether they keep doing it depends on one measurable thing: how much capability another dollar of reinforcement-learning compute still buys. This episode makes the case that this single quantity, not chips or power or networking, decides whether the build-out is sound infrastructure or stranded assets, using the ScaleRL results, Epoch's compute figures, the CoreWeave and Oracle financings, and what would prove the argument wrong. The finale of the AI-compute series.

item.title: AI Compute 8: How a Frontier Model Is Trained
item.description: The training run that produces a named model is a small share of the computing a frontier lab spends. Epoch AI put OpenAI's 2024 final training runs at about a tenth of its research compute; the rest went to experiments. This episode explains what the rest is: the run as a system engineered to survive a hardware failure every few hours, the experiments that never ship, and the reinforcement-learning stage that now dominates, where the model generates attempts at checkable tasks and is trained on the ones that work, on an S-shaped curve whose ceiling the labs guard.

item.title: Co-Packaged Optics 2: Light Reaches the Chip on Two Clocks, Not One
item.description: On March 12, 2026, AMD, Broadcom, NVIDIA, Meta, Microsoft and OpenAI signed one specification for optical interconnect soldered permanently inside AI machines. The same spring, NVIDIA shipped a five-meter machine held together by copper and light at once. This episode argues that demand and qualification, not energy, set the dates for light's move inward, and names the one number at GTC in March 2027 that tests the claim.

item.title: AI Compute 6: Power Delivery and Cooling Inside the Data Center
item.description: A single NVIDIA NVL72 rack draws about 120 kilowatts, and a large AI data center holds thousands of them. The building's two jobs, delivering that power to the chips and carrying the heat away, have both forced it to be rebuilt: liquid cooling because air can no longer remove the heat, and 800-volt DC power because the current at these densities is otherwise unmanageable. This episode explains both, the 120-to-600-to-1000-kilowatt rack trajectory and what each step breaks, and why the building is the one part of the system whose cost is rising while everything inside it falls.

item.title: AI Compute 5: How Tens of Thousands of Chips Become One Computer
item.description: A frontier model is too large for one GPU, so it is split across tens of thousands of them that must exchange results at every step, and the speed of that exchange, not the speed of the chips, now sets the performance. This episode explains the two networks that do it: NVLink inside NVIDIA's 72-GPU rack, and InfiniBand or Ethernet between racks. It covers the copper reach limit that forces co-packaged optics in 2028, the optical-transceiver supply chain and its laser bottleneck, why one slow link stalls a 100,000-GPU training run, and why only about 40% of a cluster's compute reaches the model.

item.title: AI Compute Thesis (superseded): Why AI Automates Some Jobs and Not Others
item.description: Upstart's annual report says 91% of its loans are now made with no human involved. Insurers reject an AI's hospital billing codes a third as often as the human coders'. OpenAI charges ten times more per token for the model that checks its own answers. This episode argues those are the same fact: machines take over work where the output is cheap to check, and stall where it isn't, no matter how capable the models get. It ends with a number due in September that will test the claim. Second of two episodes on AI compute.

item.title: Verda Internal Investment Thesis: What the Series B Deck Changes
item.description: An internal, committed view of whether Verda, a Helsinki GPU cloud, can become a $10 billion company, updated against the company's own June 2026 Series B materials. An earlier version, built on roughly fifty expert-call transcripts, concluded Verda was the right shape in the wrong position: disciplined and cheap on power, but outside the chain that pulls a neocloud to scale. The company's fundraise materials claim the opposite on nearly every point: launch-partner allocation on NVIDIA's next platform, an anchor-grade foundation-lab contract, utilization and net retention well above break-even, a real power pipeline, and AI-native growth customers. This episode works through what the deck answers, what it leaves to verify, and the central thing it changes: Verda is now choosing the leveraged, asset-backed scaling path it was previously praised for avoiding. It lands on the handful of questions that decide whether the claims hold and whether a roughly seventeen-billion-euro capital plan is financeable before the depreciation and custom-silicon cycle turns. Internal investment view; company-stated figures are unaudited.

item.title: Co-Packaged Optics 1: Why AI Computers Switch from Copper to Light (register pass)
item.description: Register-pass revision of the co-packaged-optics primer, rewritten to the invisible-narrator standard (the Sensofusion 'The Machine' calibration). Same content and numbers as the public version; the narration no longer addresses the listener or narrates its own structure. Draft for the director's listen.

item.title: Sensofusion 3: When There Is Nothing to Jam
item.description: The third episode is the argument. The world's dominant way of stopping drones treats each one as a small busy radio: hear it, find it, jam the link to its pilot. The offense has spent three years deliberately leaving the radio, on three separate axes at once (fiber-optic control, onboard autonomy, and encryption), and the company's own chief research officer says so in public. This episode takes four widely-held beliefs about counter-drone and corrects each with the mechanism: that detection is the hard part (it isn't; defeat and the authority to act are); that jamming defeats drones (the threat is being designed to be unjammable); that a wall or one clever system stops drones (the cost-exchange forces cheap layered mass and an integrating command system, and single sensors are becoming swappable feeds); and that the exquisite prime systems win, or that it's all a war bubble (cheap attritable mass wins the small-drone tier, and the demand has a structural floor under a cyclical premium). It lands on a committed five-year view (the threat goes dark and mass, defeat migrates from the link to the airframe, the decision layer goes autonomous out of necessity, and value concentrates at the command layer and the cheap effector) and where Sensofusion sits on it, with the things that would prove each call wrong.

item.title: ICEYE 3: Why the Sharpest Radar Doesn't Win
item.description: The third episode is the argument. There is a way to rank radar-satellite companies that feels obviously right, by how sharp a picture each one takes, and it predicts the wrong winner: by that scoreboard ICEYE is third, and third is winning the market. This episode works through why, by taking apart four widely-held beliefs about the field and letting a committed view of the technology fall out of the corrections. That resolution is the contest (it is walled, and the wall is a spectrum regulation, not physics). That radar can track moving things like video (it cannot, and the one real frontier for fixing that is flying satellites in coherent pairs, not building a sharper radar). That you are buying images (you are increasingly buying answers, and the value is leaving the sensor for the layer that fuses and delivers them). And that the sovereign-buying wave is a defense bubble (the signed core is structural; the commercial edge and the marginal deals are not). Where the most relevant technologies and products actually go over the next five years, and the things that would prove each call wrong.

item.title: Verda 3: The Chip Was Never the Hard Part
item.description: The third episode is the argument. The whole AI-compute boom is read through the chip, and the chip is the one part of the system that commoditizes and depreciates fastest. This episode corrects four beliefs with the mechanism and lets a committed five-year view fall out. That the bottleneck is chips (it crossed to power: grid queues over four years, transformers over two, turbines sold out to the end of the decade, and the people running the buildouts saying they have chips they cannot plug in). That NVIDIA wins forever (the CUDA moat holds in training and erodes in inference, where serving software iterates weekly and custom silicon is aimed first, though a merchant cloud can still only buy NVIDIA and AMD and rides the roadmap as a price-taker). That it is a training boom (it is an inference and reasoning boom, with reasoning burning far more compute per query, against an efficiency curve falling fast the other way). And that a neocloud is a money-printer or a pure commodity (it is the hollowed middle of a barbell, where operational quality earns a premium but only owning power or climbing the stack earns an escape, and the real fragility is the financing, not the demand). Where Verda sits on that map, capability by capability, and the four things that would prove the view wrong. No financials.

item.title: Sensofusion 2: Anyone Can Spot a Drone. Few Can Stop One.
item.description: Why counter-drone defense is mission-critical, the full menu of ways to stop a drone (radio, radar, cameras, sound, jamming, takeover, guns, interceptor drones, and high-power microwave), and where the durable value actually sits. A capability-and-architecture view of the field Sensofusion competes in, with a committed view of where the threat and the defense are headed.

item.title: ICEYE 2: The Same Radar, Sold Five Ways
item.description: Why all-weather, day-and-night, frequently-refreshed radar intelligence is mission-critical, and why governments stopped renting it and started owning it. The full menu of ways to get ground truth from space (optical cameras, free open radar, truck-sized agency radar, the small-radar rivals, aircraft, and other sensing types), the five structurally different transactions ICEYE runs on one instrument (a data subscription, a transfer of control, a whole-satellite sale, a turnkey sovereign system, and a factory on the buyer's own soil), and a committed view of where the durable value sits. ICEYE is third on raw sharpness behind Umbra and Capella and wins anyway, on revisit, speed, and sovereign ownership. Where the field is heading, with the thing that would prove each claim wrong.

item.title: Verda 2: The Same Chip, a Different Cloud
item.description: Why almost everyone rents AI compute instead of owning it (the cost of a cluster, the depreciation bet on a chip superseded yearly, and the utilization that bursty AI work rarely reaches), the menu of where to get it (hyperscalers, neoclouds, building your own, and the chip choice underneath), and what actually separates the winners. The chip is common, but the speed and reliability a cloud delivers on it are not: on identical GPUs, achieved performance and uptime vary widely, and buyers pay large premiums for the better operators on the same hardware. So an AI cloud is a performance product, not a commodity, and a well-run focused operator can win and keep demanding customers. Where Verda fits, with its real strengths and real limits, and where the market is heading.

item.title: AI Compute Overview: How the Whole Machine Gets Built
item.description: The supply chain behind one AI query: an $8 million rack in northern Virginia, wafers from TSMC, lithography machines from ASML (about sixty a year, for the whole planet), stacked memory from SK Hynix, and electricity bought three years ahead. How each piece works, why the bottleneck keeps moving from one step to another, and where the money pools. First of two episodes on AI compute.

item.title: ICEYE 1: Too Small to Work, and It Works Anyway
item.description: An ICEYE satellite weighs about eighty-five kilograms, makes its own microwave illumination, and draws pictures of the ground through cloud and darkness. This episode follows the radar end to end: why spaceborne radar was historically the size of a truck, the one clause in the physics that lets a satellite go small, the two separate sharpnesses of a radar image, what a twenty-five-second stare actually buys, and where the small antenna goes blind, including why it cannot track a moving target.

item.title: Verda 1: Ten Thousand GPUs, One Computer
item.description: What a customer of Verda, a GPU cloud, is actually buying: a single GPU and why a model is too big for one, eight of them wired into one server, thousands wired into one computer across two very different networks, the building that delivers the power and removes the heat, and the software stack that drives all of it — the scheduler, the kernels, the failure-recovery, the serving layer. Then the part that decides the purchase: the levels you can buy at, from a bare machine to a finished model behind an API, who buys each and why; why a training job and an inference job want different hardware; and why two clouds running the identical NVIDIA chips deliver very different speed and reliability, which is what a serious buyer is really choosing between.
